articles.text:
How the Grand Canyon could have lost 1 billion years of geologic history
Skip to content
Subscribe today
Every print subscription comes with full digital access
Subscribe Now
By Lucas Van Wyk Joel
October 9, 2026 at 11:00 am
Share this:
Share
Share via email (Opens in new window)
Email
Share on Facebook (Opens in new window)
Facebook
Share on Reddit (Opens in new window)
Reddit
Share on X (Opens in new window)
Print (Opens in new window)
Print
In the Grand Canyon, rock layers preserve a relatively continuous record of Earth’s geologic history going back about 2 billion years. But between 520 million and 1.8 billion years, the record is noticeably empty. It’s as if someone broke into a museum and made off with almost an entire wing’s worth of rocks, and sorting out “whodunnit” is one of the coldest cases in all geology.
Now, scientists studying the Grand Canyon’s rocks say that a gigantic Earth-spanning cliff  —with a global glaciation as its accomplice — could be to blame for the heist.
The giant cliff started forming about 800 million years ago as an ancient supercontinent called Rodinia split apart, Thomas Gernon, an earth scientist at the University of Southampton in England, and colleagues report August 17 in Geology. Forces like rain and ice weathered and eroded the rock and, like waves at the beach steadily erasing one layer of sand after another, deleted a billion years of Earth’s history.
The group used computer models to simulate how ancient Earth evolved over hundreds of millions of years. They watched as the cliff — known as an escarpment — formed around the time in Earth’s history when rocks in the region vanished.
The escarpment most likely extended across much of a continent called Laurentia, the ancient precursor to North America. It stretched from what was to become Alaska all the way to Arizona and would have been about one to two kilometers high.
Spanning a continent
Some 65 million years ago, the Great Escarpment of Laurentia would have stretched across much of North America, including the spot that would one day become the Grand Canyon and the site of an enduring geologic mystery. The escarpment itself is thought to have formed around 800 million years ago.
T.M. Gernon et al/Geology, 2026; Ron Blakey/Deep Time Maps
“No study has previously suggested the existence of a continental-scale escarpment in the Grand Canyon region. Our study shows it’s a plausible, straightforward explanation for the immense erosion that took place in the Grand Canyon,” Gernon says. Such an immense cliff created steep slopes that were ideal places for the elements to loosen and make off with exposed rock.
And the escarpment had a lot of help when it came to its disappearing act: ice, lots and lots of ice. The theft of the rocks coincided with an extreme period of glaciation called Snowball Earth. Massive ice sheets formed and may have extended all the way from the poles to equatorial latitudes. As the ice expanded, it would have eroded great quantities of rock, helping create the gap in the record.
And the escarpment, due to its high elevation, would have created ideal conditions for Snowball Earth glaciers and ice sheets to form. In a separate study published in Science, Gernon and a team explained how an escarpment created by tectonic activity was responsible for the formation of the East Antarctic Ice Sheet starting some 34 million years ago. “The exposed rocky peaks of the escarpment would have acted as glacier factories,” Gernon says.
It remains unclear, however, whether the erosion that erased the rocks occurred before, during or after the Snowball Earth glaciations. “That’s the real hole that needs filling: pinning down the erosion history in space and time, continent by continent, precisely enough,” Gernon says.
Linking the disappearance of the rocks to verified events in Earth’s history such as the breakup of Rodinia bolsters the case, says Alan Collins, a geologist at Adelaide University in Australia who was not involved in the new study. Not only that, but Gernon’s team points to modern-day examples where similar erosive processes are at work, including a similar escarpment in Antarctica as well as one in South Africa.
Maybe not quite case closed yet, but “I find this very convincing,” Collins says.

Here’s a look at the Nobel Prizes for science
Skip to content
Subscribe today

By Nikk Ogasa

Share this:
Share

Email

Facebook
Share on Reddit (Opens in new window)
Reddit

Print
It’s Nobels season — that time of the year when we find out which groundbreaking, paradigm-shifting, world-changing achievements beat out the rest to win what is arguably the most prestigious award on Earth.
From a light switch for the brain to the discovery of an ultra-elusive subatomic particle hailing from beyond our solar system to a solution to one of the most enduring puzzles in all of organic chemistry, the researchers behind this year’s scientific prizes each revolutionized the ways that scientists understand the world around them.
Take a look at the science behind each of this year’s awards.
Shining a light
A galaxy of nearly 90 billion neurons exists within a single human brain. But unlike stars in the void, neurons communicate with one another via some 100 trillion connections, allowing the human mind to learn, adapt and interact with its surroundings.
For scientists to understand how individual actions arise from such complexity, they needed a tool to directly link neural circuits to specific behaviors, said Abdel El Manira, a neuroscientist at the Karolinska Institute in Stockholm. “Neuroscientists dreamed of a neuronal switch, a tool to turn specific neurons on or off with great precision,” El Manira said during the Oct. 5 announcement of this year’s prize in physiology or medicine by the Nobel Assembly at Karolinska Institute.
Enter the bright idea that won. It’s a technology called optogenetics, which involves using light to precisely activate specific cells, like neurons, and watch how behavior changes. For their foundational contributions to optogenetics, biophysicists Peter Hegemann of Humboldt University in Berlin and Georg Nagel, of the Julius-Maximilians-Universität Würzburg in Germany, and neuroscientist Karl Deisseroth of Stanford University shared this year’s prize.
Karl Deisseroth (left), Peter Hegemann (middle) and Georg Nagel (right) have won the 2026 Nobel Prize in physiology or medicine for their creation of optogenetics. Niklas Elmehed © Nobel Prize Outreach
The prize winners’ story starts in an unlikely place: the eye spot of a single celled green alga called Chlamydomonas. In the early 2000s, Hegemann, then at the Max Planck Institute for Biochemistry in Martinsreid, Germany, and Nagel, at the Max Planck Institute for Biophysics in Frankfurt, discovered a unique protein in the alga’s eye spot. When illuminated, the protein generated an electrical impulse, enabling the organism to move. Further research revealed that when the protein, called channelrhodopsin, was exposed to light, it opened like a pore, allowing positively charged ions to flow into a cell, generating the electrical impulse. “They had just discovered the switch neuroscientists had long dreamed of,” El Manira said.
Building on the Hegemann and Nagel’s work, Deisseroth began testing whether channelrhodopsin could be used to activate brain cells. He and his colleagues first inserted the gene for channelrhodopsin into cultures of rat nerve cells and found that the cells reacted to light instantaneously. They then introduced the gene into nerve cells in the brains of living mice, along with optical fibers fed through the rodents’ skulls. By beaming blue light through the fibers, the researchers were able to control the movements of the rodents’ whiskers. This technology gave researchers the ability to test the links between certain brain circuits and behaviors.
Optogenetics is a technology that lets scientists precisely activate specific cells using light, thereby allowing them to turn on specific brain circuits and watch for changes in behavior.© The Nobel Committee for Physiology or Medicine. Ill. Mattias Karlén
“The technology, which soon became known as optogenetics, transformed neuroscience,” El Manira said. In addition to exposing the inner workings of healthy brains, he noted, “it has also helped reveal how brain circuits are disrupted, with implications for conditions such as blindness, depression and dementia.”
For example, the technology has been used improve vision in some patients with retinitis pigmentosa, a disease that degrades light-sensing cells in the retina. It’s also helping researchers investigate the role that a person’s heart plays in how they experience and interact with their surroundings.
Capturing a ghost
At the South Pole, there exists a block of ice unlike any other on Earth. Buried deep beneath the surface of the Antarctic ice sheet, a cubic kilometer of ice is threaded with thousands of beadlike sensors. Known as the IceCube Neutrino Observatory, this immense instrument enables researchers to detect the most elusive particle in the universe — the neutrino.
Detecting neutrinos from beyond our solar system had been a goal of scientists for decades, as that could help understand where and how the universe accelerates particles to extraordinary energies.
Francis Halzen won this year’s Nobel Prize in physics for his vision and leadership in establishing the IceCube Neutrino Observatory in Antarctica, which discovered high-energy neutrinos from beyond the solar system. Niklas Elmehed © Nobel Prize Outreach
The researcher who led the creation of the Antarctic observatory, physicist Francis Halzen of the University of Wisconsin–Madison, received this year’s Nobel Prize in physics. Halzen was awarded “for his decisive contributions to the IceCube Neutrino Observatory and the discovery of high-energy neutrinos of astrophysical origin,” Mark Pearce, a physicist and chair of the Nobel committee for physics, during the Oct. 6 announcement by the Royal Swedish Academy of Sci

articles.title: Kilauea's display is revealing why volcanoes spew like a fountain show
articles.text:
Kilauea's display is revealing why volcanoes spew like a fountain show
Skip to content

Subscribe Now
By Carolyn Gramling
October 8, 2026 at 2:05 pm
Share this:
Share
Share via email (Opens in new window)
Email
Share on Facebook (Opens in new window)
Facebook
Share on Reddit (Opens in new window)
Reddit
Share on X (Opens in new window)
Print (Opens in new window)
Print
Kilauea has been erupting almost continuously for nearly 200 years, and volcanologists have seen a lot of sides to Hawaii’s most active volcano. But in the last year, Kilauea started doing something new: firing up frequent fountains of lava.
The volcano’s fountain era kicked off at dawn on December 23, 2024, with an eruption inside the summit crater of Halema’uma’u. Since then, Kilauea has put on a recurring pyrotechnic display of lava fountains, researchers report October 8 in Science. It produced 54 different lava fountains by September 2026, some of which shot as high as 457 meters into the sky.
During an eruption, which can last from hours to days, months or even years, occasional lava fountains aren’t unusual. But it’s rare to see repeated fountains — distinct bursts separated by minutes to weeks — during a single eruption. At Kilauea, these clustered spurts have only occurred three times since 1823, and never with such frequency.
Thanks to their rarity, researchers have known relatively little about what initiates, sustains and ends these episodic fountains, say Ashton Flinders, a research geophysicist at the U.S. Geological Survey’s Hawaiian Volcano Observatory, based in Hilo, and colleagues. There have been two prevailing ideas: Water dissolved in magma — the underground, molten mix of rock and gas — rising from deep inside the volcano suddenly escapes as the pressure changes, leading to a burst of pyrotechnics; or a carbon dioxide–rich foam atop the trapped magma, like the pressurized froth over a shaken bottle of soda, suddenly and violently expands.
Kilauea is the perfect laboratory in which to assess these hypotheses, the researchers say. It has been intensely studied by scientists and monitored by instruments for decades. Scientists continuously collect data on its seismic activity, temperature, low-frequency acoustics, how much the ground swells or deflates and the gases that escape. Using these data, researchers have begun to form a picture of what’s causing the relentless spewing.
Before each fountain, the team found, the floor of the bowl-shaped caldera would swell and tilt, suggesting magma was gathering beneath. As the eruption matured and the fountains continued, a pattern emerged, first appearing before the fourteenth fountain. Just before that eruption, the team detected a repetitive sequence of minutes-long bursts of seismic energy and low-frequency acoustics.
Those signals, the researchers say, are linked to the buildup and release of trapped gases in magma, which make it rise and fall through narrow volcanic vents in the rock like a piston in a car. The team also noted that while the volcano burped some sulfur dioxide gas, there was relatively little carbon dioxide, suggesting that the foam hypothesis wasn’t at work.
This is just a preliminary glimpse into this phenomenon, and a lot of questions remain, Flinders and his colleagues say.

An experimental drug kills fat cells, rather than shrinking them
Skip to content
Subscribe today
Every print subscription comes with full digital access
Subscribe Now
By Tina Hesman Saey
October 8, 2026 at 9:00 am
Share this:
Share
Share via email (Opens in new window)
Email
Share on Facebook (Opens in new window)
Facebook
Share on Reddit (Opens in new window)
Reddit
Share on X (Opens in new window)
Print (Opens in new window)
Print
An experimental drug may melt away a dangerous type of fat that packs around internal organs.
The drug, called CBL-514, specifically triggers fat cells to enter a death program called apoptosis. People who got injections of the experimental drug in their lower abdomens lost visceral fat, researchers reported October 1 at the annual meeting of the European Association for the Study of Diabetes in Milan, Italy. Visceral fat sits deep in the abdomen where it chokes organs and can spur inflammation and health problems.
Weight loss can shrink fat cells, but the cells are still there, poised to balloon up again.
The team already knew the experimental drug could reduce subcutaneous fat, the pinchable fat that sits under the skin, in the abdomen. That surface fat doesn’t carry the same health risks that visceral fat does.
In the new study, researchers examined MRIs from a subset of participants in two small clinical trials to track visceral fat levels. Study participants, who ranged from healthy weights to overweight, got injections of CBL-514 or placebo every three weeks for up to 12 weeks. The two groups started with about the same amount of visceral fat; 642.5 milliliters on average in the CBL-514 group and 677.4 milliliters in the placebo group. Four weeks after treatment, those who got the experimental drug had dropped almost 71 mL of visceral fat (a 12 percent decrease), while the placebo group gained 31 mL (a nearly 6 percent increase) of the dangerous fat in their abdomens.
Measurements taken at eight to 12 weeks after treatment showed the gap had widened. Those who got the experimental drug lost almost 63 mL — about a quarter cup — of visceral fat on average while the placebo group gained more than 78 mL of visceral fat over the starting point. Those results suggest that the drug might have health benefits by reducing visceral fat, which contributes to diabetes and heart problems. Larger clinical trials to test efficacy and safety of the drug are ongoing.

here .)
Some blind people can now find a doorway or spot an object with the help of an experimental treatment and custom goggles.
Participants in a new study had blindness caused by a genetic disease called retinitis pigmentosa, which progressively kills off light-sensing cells in the retina. The treatment improved seven of 10 people’s light sensitivity, researchers report October 7 in New England Journal of Medicine. The findings build on a 2021 report that the same approach helped one blind man see and count objects.
The treatment is based on optogenetics, a technique that uses genetic instructions to make cells respond to light. Rather than repair the retina’s damaged light detectors, it gives that ability to retinal ganglion cells that normally relay visual signals to the brain.
“This is a proof of concept that optogenetics can bring back some visual activity [and] object sensitivity,” says Botond Roska, neuroscientist at the Institute of Molecular and Clinical Ophthalmology Basel in Switzerland.
Pioneering work on optogenetics snagged the 2026 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine on October 5.
The treatment and goggles gave some blind people the ability to detect objects by turning images, like this hand, into light patterns that activate retinal cells.Dr. Chloé Pagot, Ph.D., Streetlab, Paris
Scientists have been experimenting with optogenetic therapies to rewire the eye and restore vision to people with degenerative eye diseases for more than a decade. Just as in the 2021 study, in the new work Roska and his colleagues injected genetic instructions for ChrimsonR, a light-sensitive protein derived from algae, into participants’ worse-seeing eye. The treatment made retinal ganglion cells in that eye sensitive to amber light. A camera in the custom goggles detected changes in brightness in what was in front of a study participant, and the goggles projected those changes onto the retina as pulses of amber light, activating the treated cells.
Four of the eight study participants who completed behavioral testing after treatment were able to find a doorway or follow a line while wearing the goggles. No patient gained the ability to read visual words or see faces, but Roska and his colleagues hope to tackle that next.
But there’s a limitation to this work. The approach requires a working optic nerve to carry signals to the brain, says study coauthor José-Alain Sahel, an ophthalmologist at the University of Pittsburgh. It relies on cells in the retina communicating to the brain, so it cannot restore vision when that connection is damaged.

Alzheimer’s damage may begin outside the brain

Destructive immune cells tied to Alzheimer’s disease may get their marching orders from cells outside the brain rather than within it.
In mice, suppressing a small population of immune cells located in lymph nodes protects against neurodegeneration, researchers report September 3 in Nature Neuroscience. The findings raise the possibility of treating Alzheimer’s disease while bypassing the brain’s siege defenses.
For years, researchers have gone all in on efforts to remove toxic tangles of proteins like amyloid and tau from the brain as a way of halting Alzheimer’s, with limited success. But the immune system also plays an important role in neurodegeneration. What exactly that role is — protector or antagonist — has been unclear.
In 2023, neurologist David Holtzman and colleagues showed that immune system T cells accumulate around tau tangles — implying that they might cause damage. Halting these cells’ entry into the brain reduced inflammation, and also reduced neuronal damage, says Holtzman, of Washington University School of Medicine in St. Louis.
Still, it wasn’t known how these T cells accessed the brain in the first place. “A big question has been whether the T cells passively enter the brain or are primed … to do so,” says Rudolph Tanzi, a neurogeneticist at Harvard Medical School who wasn’t involved in the study.
During priming, T cells are ordered to rally and multiply. The generals that bark out these orders are called dendritic cells, which capture signatures of cellular threats called antigens and present them to T cell infantry.
No one had looked closely at what dendritic cells in lymph nodes were doing during neurodegenerative disease, Holtzman says. So in the new study, he and his colleagues compared two groups of mice engineered to have tau-linked neurodegeneration, one of which lacked dendritic cells.
Blocking an attack
Alzheimer’s-like neurodegeneration can ravage a brain, as seen in the slice of a mouse’s brain at left. The attack may be planned in the lymph nodes, new research suggests. The brain slice depicted on the right came from a mouse in which that early stage of attack was blocked.
Courtesy Hao Hu
In old age, mice without dendritic cells still had brains packed with tau. But compared with the other mice, they were protected against neurodegeneration and performed better on cognitive tasks like nest building.
They also had far fewer T cells in their brains. This suggests that tau tangles aren’t working alone in driving neurodegeneration, Holtzman says. “A lot of the damage that tau is causing is due to the inflammatory response that it’s eliciting.” The results would need to be replicated in human brains, he adds.
Despite this seemingly important role, the researchers found few dendritic cells in the mice’s brains. Instead, they detected threat-mimicking brain proteins traveling to the lymph nodes, where dendritic cells used them to rally T cells. The team bred mutant mice with demoted dendritic cell generals that could no longer give commands to T cells. These mice also had fewer T cells in their brains and better-preserved brain structures.
It isn’t practical to disable dendritic cells from birth in people at risk of Alzheimer’s. But Holtzman says his colleagues are working on cellular targets that could suppress them in adulthood. The real promise of the study may be a dementia treatment that bypasses the nervous system’s locked vault — the blood-brain barrier, Holtzman says. “If this panned out, potentially you wouldn’t have to get [therapeutics] into the brain.”

First series of adult T. rex footprints hints at its walking speed

Four ancient footprints are helping scientists step into a T. rex’s shoes.
The prints form the  first set of tracks probably left behind by an adult Tyrannosaurus rex, researchers report September 8 in the Journal of Vertebrate Paleontology. Measurements of the 7-meter-long trackway suggest the  ancient predator was ambling along at about 1.6 meters per second, roughly equivalent to a person’s quick walking pace.
A few single adult T. rex footprints exist in the fossil record, as do trackways possibly from T. rex juveniles or  other dinosaur species, says Peter Falkingham, a paleontologist at Liverpool John Moores University in England. “But an individual track doesn’t tell you a lot. A trackway tells you more about foot placement as the animal’s moving along.” And younger and older dinosaurs probably walked differently, just as human toddlers and adults do.
“Finding an adult trackway is cool,” Falkingham says. “It’s unique. It brings something new.”
High school teacher and paleontologist Kent Hups stumbled on the footprints in 2025, while fossil hunting along a steep incline in the Hell Creek Formation in North Dakota. The tracks stick up out of the ground because sediment filled in the originally muddy footprints, which then eroded away more slowly than the surrounding rock.
When Hups saw the first track, he noted that it was three-toed and enormous, measuring 80 centimeters across. “I’m going, ‘this has to be a T. rex,’” says Hups, of Northglenn High School in Colo. and the Denver Museum of Nature and Science.
Four Tyrannosaurus rex footprints, shown from above in a drone photo (left), make up the first discovered trackway left behind by an adult. The frontmost footprint (right) is the best preserved and has three distinct toes.K. Hups
Slender toe impressions and fossils unearthed in the area signal a T. rex left behind the footprints roughly 66.5 million years ago. “There’s always the possibility that we haven’t found the skeletons of some species that we don’t know about,” Falkingham says. “But as far as our knowledge goes, T. rex is about the only track maker that could have made these.”
The team used stride length and body size to calculate the dinosaur’s speed. Unfortunately, the footprints aren’t well-preserved and estimating  speed from tracks is tricky, so the T. rex may have  been walking slightly faster or slower than calculated. Better tracks could have revealed whether the foot landed flat or toe-to-heel, or how foot pads supported the predator’s weight.
More tracks are sure to follow. In fact, a fifth step may be concealed in the hill. But the team is waiting for Mother Nature to wear away the surrounding rock, Hups says. “I can’t wait to get back out there and keep looking for more.”

Meet the newest living cat species, the first described in 100 years

Attention cat lovers: There’s an adorable new addition to the feline family tree.
Meet Leopardus tilcayo, a pint-size tiger cat discovered in Bolivia in the Yungas forests of the central Andes Mountains. L. tilcayo, reported September 17 in Current Biology, is the first new living cat species described and named by scientists in more than 100 years. The last one was the Uruguayan pampas cat (L. fasciatus), described in 1923.
L. tilcayo has a slender body, spotted fur and a ringed tail. It weighs roughly two kilograms, about as much as a two-month-old domestic kitten. For such a tiny cat, L. tilcayo has made a terrific splash, pouncing into headlines around the world. “I did not at all expect attention at this scale,” says Jonas Lescroart, an evolutionary biologist at the University of Antwerp in Belgium.
Tigrino, shown here, belongs to the new species L. tilcayo. He’s about 10 years old and lived as a house pet for a year before coming to a sanctuary in Bolivia.Paola Nogales-Ascarrunz/PIF_Bolivia
Lescroart and his colleagues hadn’t set out to discover a new species. They were looking to untangle one branch of the cat family tree. Until now, scientists didn’t have a good sense of how many tiger cat species existed. These small cats live in the tropical regions of the Americas and tend to look alike, Lescroart says.
The researchers analyzed the genetics of 38 species of the Leopardus genus, which includes tiger cats as well as more widely known animals like the ocelot. They expected to find two, three or even four distinct species of tiger cat. Instead, Lescroart and his colleagues’ analyses pointed to five separate species, including one that scientists had never before described: L. tilcayo.
The new species is based on two specimens: a female that was treated briefly for injuries at a sanctuary in Bolivia and released to the wild and a male that still lives at the sanctuary. His name is Tigrino. Lescroart’s colleague, Paola Nogales-Ascarrunz, met Tigrino at the sanctuary and noticed that he looked a little different from the cats she expected to see in the region. Nogales-Ascarrunz, a cat conservationist and National Geographic Explorer, genetically tested Tigrino and then connected with Lescroart’s team to share data.
The researchers’ work suggests that there’s diversity hiding even among well-studied animals like cats. “I don’t know if you’ll have to wait another 100 years for a new species,” Lescroart says. Though at the moment, the team doesn’t have any other cryptic kitties on the radar.
